## The big idea

Pressure is a **scalar** — one number per point, no direction — that
*manifests* as a force wherever there's a surface, real or imaginary,
always pushing normal to it. Get that distinction straight now and the
whole of Unit 3 is bookkeeping. (Surface tension, meanwhile, is the
property that takes over when things get small.)

## Think first

**Recall**

1. Newton's second and third laws — you'll see both in one molecular argument below.
2. What is density? Roughly what is it for water? For the air in this room?

**Look ahead**

1. If pressure has no direction, why does it push on things in a definite direction?
2. What is *gauge* pressure, and why does an engineer in Boulder care about the number 83,000?
3. When does surface tension matter, and when can we ignore it entirely?

## Pressure: a scalar that pushes

Here is the molecular picture, for a gas. A molecule strikes a wall and
bounces off: its velocity changed, so it accelerated, so (Newton's second
law) the wall pushed on it — and (Newton's third law) it pushed on the
wall. For an elastic bounce the velocity change is entirely along the
wall's normal, so the push is too: **pressure acts perpendicular to
surfaces**, always. Sum a mole's worth of bounces per second and you have
a steady, macroscopic force per area.[^liquids]

[^liquids]: For liquids the story is messier at the molecular level —
liquid molecules are essentially in contact, and it takes enormous force
to push them even slightly closer. That's why liquid pressure can rise
dramatically with almost no density change, which is what we mean when we
call a liquid *incompressible*.

Now the crucial abstraction: we promote pressure from a wall-interaction
to a property of the fluid *itself*, defined at every point — $p(x, t)$,
a scalar. Drop an imaginary surface anywhere into the fluid, at any
orientation, and the fluid on each side pushes on it, normal to it, with
magnitude $p \times$ area. Pressure itself has no direction; the *surface
you ask about* supplies one. That's why we can speak of "the pressure at
a point" without saying which way — it's the same number for every
orientation of the test surface. (This isotropy is provable, not just
plausible; the argument is a tiny force balance on a wedge of fluid, and
it's in the collapsed box below if you want it.)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Click here for the wedge argument (why pressure is direction-free).

Take a small triangular prism of static fluid with legs $\Delta x$,
$\Delta z$ and hypotenuse at angle $\theta$. Pressure pushes normal to
each face: $p_x$ on the vertical face, $p_z$ on the horizontal, $p_n$ on
the slanted one. Force balance in $x$: $p_x \Delta z = p_n \Delta s
\sin\theta = p_n \Delta z$, so $p_x = p_n$. Balance in $z$ gives $p_z =
p_n$ plus a weight term that vanishes as the wedge shrinks. Since
$\theta$ was arbitrary: one pressure, all directions.
:::

**Absolute vs gauge.** Pressure is fundamentally thermodynamic (it and
one more state variable pin down a gas's state), and thermodynamics
demands the *absolute* number. But mechanics only ever feels pressure
*differences* — a submarine hull cares about outside-minus-inside — so we
usually measure from a convenient reference:

$$p_\text{absolute} = p_\text{reference} + p_\text{gauge}.$$

The reference is almost always the local atmosphere: about 101,300 Pa at
sea level, and about **83,000 Pa here in Boulder** — a number worth
memorizing, because it's the one that will bite you in Unit 8 when
cavitation calculations demand absolute pressure and you reflexively type
101325. Saying "the air around us is at zero (gauge)" makes the math
easier and is mechanically harmless; just know which currency you're in
before you convert.

## Surface tension: the small-scale specialist

At a liquid's surface, molecules are pulled inward by neighbors they
don't have on the air side; the surface acts like a stretched membrane
with tension $\sigma$ (about 0.073 N/m for clean water). Per unit
*volume* this force is puny — but it scales with *length* while weight
scales with length *cubed*, so shrink the problem and surface tension
wins. The crossover is around a millimeter for water; below it live
droplets, capillary rise, and insects that walk on ponds.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof D_cap12 = Inputs.range([0.2, 10], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Tube inner diameter (mm)"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - D_cap12
sigma, rho, theta = 0.0728, 998.2, 0.0
D = D_cap12/1000
h_rise = 4*sigma*np.cos(theta)/(rho*9.81*D)
Ds = np.linspace(0.2e-3, 10e-3, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(Ds*1000, 4*sigma/(rho*9.81*Ds)*1000, lw=2.5)
ax.plot(D*1000, h_rise*1000, 'o', ms=11, mfc='gold', mec='k')
ax.set_xlabel('tube diameter (mm)'); ax.set_ylabel('capillary rise (mm)')
ax.set_title(f"water climbs {h_rise*1000:.1f} mm in a {D_cap12:g} mm tube  (h = 4σ/ρgD)")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Slide toward small: at 0.2 mm the climb is ~15 cm — this is how paper
towels and tree capillaries operate. Slide toward 10 mm and the effect is
a rounding error; that's why none of Units 3–8 will mention $\sigma$
again, and *when to ignore a physical effect* is exactly the judgment
module 2.1 will make systematic.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"Pressure pushes down." Pressure pushes on *surfaces*, normal to them,
whichever way they face — down on the top of a submerged plate, **up** on
its bottom, sideways on its sides. (The *up* push on the bottom is
slightly bigger, and that imbalance has a famous name coming in 3.3.)
:::

That 10⁻⁶ is the water number you will type most often this semester (Re lives on it). One more property earns a gate:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Pressure excess inside a 2.0 mm diameter water droplet, from surface tension?"
     data-answer="146" data-tol="0.03" data-units="Pa"
     data-hint="Δp = 2σ/R for a droplet — R, the radius, is 1.0 mm. (A soap bubble would pay 4σ/R: two surfaces.)"
     data-solution="Δp = 2(0.0728)/0.001 = 146 Pa. Small drops are pressurized little tanks — and mist is furious."></div>
```

Shrink R and Δp climbs — which is why tiny bubbles dissolve, sprays atomize reluctantly, and CT-1-11's paperclip needed gentle hands.

:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** A tire gauge in Boulder reads 220 kPa. What's the absolute pressure inside — and what would the same tire's gauge read at sea level?</summary>
Absolute ≈ 220 + 83 = 303 kPa. At sea level the same air reads about 303
− 101 ≈ 202 kPa gauge. The tire didn't change; the reference did.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Why can you feel water pressure on your eardrums at the bottom of a pool, in every head orientation?</summary>
Pressure at your depth is one scalar; your eardrum supplies the surface
and its normal. Face up, down, sideways — same magnitude, always normal
to the drum.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Rank where surface tension matters: a raindrop, a bathtub, an inkjet printer nozzle, Lake Superior.</summary>
Nozzle (tens of microns — σ *dominates*), raindrop (millimeters — σ
shapes it), bathtub and lake (negligible: weight and pressure rule).
Length scale is the whole story.
</details>

## Bring to class

Be ready to defend, in one breath: pressure is a scalar — so where does
the direction of the force on a dam come from?
